title: The order of the ragas
hook: the Granth moves from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti, thirty-one ragas in a fixed order

segments.voice: Yesterday, tanti saaj, the string instruments, and your line was strings and skin. Which did you follow, the string or the drum? Today, the whole map of the ragas, start to finish. Day one thousand sixty-five.

Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri. Say them aloud and they almost sound like a line of poetry. They're the first five raga sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, in order, and the list keeps going, section after section, until it reaches Jaijavanti near the end of the book. The order is fixed. It's part of the Granth's shape. Know a hymn's raga, and you know which stretch of the book it lives in. Today: the order of the ragas.
screen: `SRI, MAJH, GAURI, ASA, GUJRI…` → `ALL THE WAY TO JAIJAVANTI.` → `A FIXED ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the list as the Granth gives it. Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri, Devgandhari, Bihagra, Vadhans, Sorath, Dhanasari, Jaitsri, Todi, Bairari, Tilang, Suhi, Bilaval, Gond, Ramkali, Nat Narayan, Mali Gaura, Maru, Tukhari, Kedara, Bhairo, Basant, Sarang, Malar, Kanara, Kalyan, Prabhati, Jaijavanti. Sikh tradition counts thirty-one main ragas, and some sections also hold mixed forms, named in their headings, like Gauri Purbi. Notice what kind of order this is. It isn't by author: Guru Nanak doesn't get a book of his own. It isn't by date. It's by sound. Open the Granth at a raga and you're inside one mood, and every voice there speaks in it. Inside each section there's a second order. The Gurus' hymns come first, by Mahala, and then the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and others, in the same raga. So a weaver of Banaras and a Guru of the Punjab can share a page, under one heading, sung in one tune. Why does the list run in this sequence and not another? The Granth doesn't say. Scholars have suggested reasons; the text itself is silent, and it's fair to leave it there. What the order does, plainly, is turn the book into a walk through moods: earnest, longing, hopeful, grieving, joyful, still. A person reading straight through doesn't just move from page to page. They move from feeling to feeling. That's today's line: thirty-one moods. Over the coming weeks this block walks the list a raga at a time, and tomorrow it begins at the beginning.
screen: `SRI TO JAIJAVANTI, IN A FIXED ORDER.` · `ORDERED BY SOUND, NOT BY AUTHOR.` · `GURUS FIRST, THEN THE BHAGATS.` · then, large: `THIRTY-ONE MOODS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the raga list. It's on your screen. Read it slowly, one name to a breath. Sri on the way in, let it go on the way out. Then Majh. Then Gauri. Don't hurry toward the end. If a name catches you, give it a second breath. You won't remember them all, and you don't need to. You're walking the length of the book by its moods. If you pray, you can let the last breath, after Jaijavanti, carry a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
screen: `SRI · MAJH · GAURI · ASA · GUJRI · DEVGANDHARI` → `BIHAGRA · VADHANS · SORATH · DHANASARI · JAITSRI` → `TODI · BAIRARI · TILANG · SUHI · BILAVAL · GOND` → `RAMKALI · NAT NARAYAN · MALI GAURA · MARU` → `TUKHARI · KEDARA · BHAIRO · BASANT · SARANG` → `MALAR · KANARA · KALYAN · PRABHATI · JAIJAVANTI`

segments.voice: The order of the ragas. A fixed path through the Granth's raga sections, Sri to Jaijavanti, ordered by sound rather than by author, with the Gurus first and the Bhagats after in each. Today's word.
screen: `THE ORDER OF THE RAGAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: thirty-one moods. Today, give three hours of your day a mood each, the way the Granth names a raga, and see how they line up. Day one thousand sixty-five.

howItsDone: In a sahaj path or akhand path, a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, readers move through the raga sections in this fixed order, from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti.

The count 'thirty-one' is in the index carry; the script attributes it to Sikh tradition, since the Granth itself doesn't number its ragas. Some counts treat mixed forms differently.
'Gurus' hymns first, by Mahala, then the Bhagats' is the general pattern; within sections hymns are also grouped by form (chaupade, ashtapadis, chhants, vars). Confirm the simplification.
'A weaver of Banaras' for Kabir follows Sikh and wider tradition; confirm.
Original set to null: no single Gurmukhi word for 'the order of the ragas' worth teaching.
Editor: cut the unsourced manuscript claim that the order never shifts between copies; now says only that the order is fixed, as the index does.
